power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background: The reduced and oxidized forms of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADPH/NADP ) connect cellular reducing power with the glutathione and thioredoxin systems.

Peripheral alterations in this network may reflect systemic redox dysregulation in Alzheimer's disease (AD) and mild cognitive impairment (MCI), but the evidence has not been quantitatively synthesized.
Objective: To systematically evaluate peripheral-blood NADP(H) redox metabolism and related enzymes in AD and MCI and to perform meta-analyses when the available data were sufficiently comparable.
Methods: PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science were searched from inception to 6 November 2026.

Eligible observational studies compared patients with AD or MCI with cognitively unimpaired controls and reported NADPH, NADP , the NADPH/NADP ratio, or NADPHrelated enzymes, including glutathione reductase (GR), glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD), and thioredoxin reductase (TRXR).
Continuous outcomes were converted to Hedges g.
Random-effects models used restricted maximum likelihood estimation and modified Hartung-Knapp confidence intervals.
Results: Of 2,686 records identified, 1,781 remained after deduplication and 13 studies were included.
No study directly reported peripheral NADPH, NADP , or the NADPH/NADP ratio.

The pooled effect for erythrocyte GR in AD was g=-1.05 (95% CI -2.73 to 0.63; I²=95.0%; five studies); for erythrocyte GR in MCI, g=-0.15 (95% CI -8.68 to 8.38; I²=95.0%; two studies); for whole-blood/plasma GR in AD, g=-0.03 (95% CI -4.37 to 4.30; I²=97.1%; three studies); and for erythrocyte G6PD in AD, g=-0.66 (95% CI -17.36 to 16.03; I²=96.4%; two studies).
Leave-one-out analyses did not materially alter the interpretation of the erythrocyte GR synthesis.
Conclusions: AD and MCI may be accompanied by remodeling of peripheral NADP(H)-related enzyme networks, but the direction and magnitude of effects are inconsistent across studies.
Direct measurement of NADPH, NADP , and their ratio remains the most important evidence gap.
Future prospective studies should standardize specimen type, pre-analytical handling, and analytical platforms and should account for disease stage, treatment exposure, and metabolic comorbidity.
Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized clinically by cognitive and functional decline.
Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) occupies an intermediate clinical space between healthy aging and dementia and is a key stage for identifying early biological changes.

Alongside amyloid-β deposition, tau pathology, synaptic dysfunction, and neuroinflammation, disruption of redox homeostasis is increasingly recognized as an integral component of AD pathobiology [15] [16] [17] 27].

text.text: Peripheral blood captures systemic metabolic, inflammatory, and antioxidant responses and therefore provides an accessible window into disease-associated biology [24] [25] [26].

text.text: The NADP(H) system is a central hub of reductive metabolism.
NADPH supplies reducing equivalents to glutathione reductase, thioredoxin reductase, and multiple antioxidant and biosynthetic reactions.

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD), the rate-controlling enzyme of the oxidative pentose phosphate pathway, contributes substantially to cytosolic NADPH regeneration, particularly in erythrocytes [21] [22] [23].

text.text: Animal, cell-culture, and brain-only studies; studies without an eligible comparator; reports restricted to oxidative-stress markers without a direct NADP(H) pathway relationship; reviews, comments, case reports, and duplicate publications were excluded.
For overlapping cohorts, the most informative report was retained.
After deduplication, titles and abstracts were screened, followed by full-text assessment.
Extracted variables included author, year, design, diagnostic group, sample size, specimen matrix, assay method, measurement unit, mean, and dispersion.
Standard errors were converted to standard deviations using SD=SEM×√n.
When an article reported multiple AD subgroups that required a single overall comparison, means and variances were combined using samplesize-weighted formulas.
Graph-only data without a reliably extractable variance were retained for narrative synthesis.
Studies with conflicting values between the main text and tables were excluded from the primary quantitative analysis and examined in scenario analyses.
Conversions and distributional approximations followed established methodological guidance where applicable [43, 44].
text.formatted: Conversions and distributional approximations followed established methodological guidance where applicable <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">[43,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">44]</ref>.

text.text: The prespecified primary outcomes were peripheral NADPH, NADP , and the NADPH/NADP ratio.
Secondary outcomes were NADPH-related enzymes, including GR, G6PD/G6PDH, and TRXR.
To limit biological non-comparability, analyses were stratified by disease stage, specimen matrix, and analyte.
Continuous outcomes were standardized as Hedges g, defined as the patient group minus the control group; negative values therefore indicate lower activity or concentration in patients.
Random-effects models used restricted maximum likelihood estimation of τ² and modified Hartung-Knapp 95% confidence intervals [38] [39] [40] [41] [42].

text.text: Leave-one-out analyses were conducted for the principal synthesis, and scenario analyses were used for internally conflicting data.
Funnel plots and Egger tests were not performed because every synthesis included fewer than 10 studies.
Analyses were conducted in R version 4.6.1.
Two-sided P<0.05 was considered statistically significant.

text.text: Discussion

GR uses NADPH to reduce oxidized glutathione, G6PD replenishes cytosolic NADPH through the pentose phosphate pathway, and TRXR transfers NADPH-derived reducing equivalents to the thioredoxin system [20] [21] [22] [23] 29, 32, 37].
text.formatted: GR uses NADPH to reduce oxidized glutathione, G6PD replenishes cytosolic NADPH through the pentose phosphate pathway, and TRXR transfers NADPH-derived reducing equivalents to the thioredoxin system <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">37]</ref>.

text.text: Lower GR may indicate impaired glutathione recycling; altered G6PD may reflect deficient NADPH supply or compensatory pathway activation; and TRXR changes may affect protein-thiol homeostasis.
Nevertheless, enzyme abundance or activity is not equivalent to the NADPH/NADP ratio.
Cofactor availability, substrate load, erythrocyte age distribution, oxidative demand, and compensatory regulation can generate opposite enzyme responses under similar net redox states.
The observed heterogeneity is therefore biologically compatible with network remodeling rather than a simple uniform depletion of antioxidant capacity.
These processes operate within broader mitochondrial and cellular redox-signaling systems [28,33-36].

4.3 Specimen matrix and clinical state as sources of heterogeneity Erythrocytes depend heavily on the pentose phosphate pathway for NADPH and lack nuclei and mitochondria; erythrocyte GR and G6PD therefore reflect a specialized intracellular redox environment.

Plasma or serum enzyme measurements may instead be influenced by cellular release, hemolysis, hepatic or renal function, and pre-analytical processing, whereas wholeblood assays combine contributions from multiple cell populations.
Matrix-specific interpretation is consequently essential.
Persistently high heterogeneity after matrix stratification further suggests contributions from disease severity, treatment exposure, nutritional status, metabolic comorbidity, and assay platform.
The treatment-associated differences reported by Klugman et al. illustrate how medication use may reshape peripheral antioxidant enzyme profiles [7].
Evidence at the MCI stage was particularly sparse.
The two erythrocyte GR studies produced effects in opposite directions and do not support GR as a stand-alone early marker.
MCI is etiologically heterogeneous, and variation in underlying amyloid and tau pathology may dilute disease-specific metabolic signals [19, 25].
text.formatted: MCI is etiologically heterogeneous, and variation in underlying amyloid and tau pathology may dilute disease-specific metabolic signals <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25]</ref>.

text.text: Studies that define MCI using established AD biomarkers and simultaneously quantify NADPH, NADP , glutathione redox couples, and pathway enzymes may be more informative than single-enzyme assays.

This multianalyte strategy is consistent with broader evidence that glutathione and lipid-peroxidation markers are altered in cognitive impairment but are strongly affected by matrix and methodology [18] [19] [20] 30, 31].

text.text: The principal contribution of this review is to define what the current evidence can-and cannot-measure.
The next phase of research should move beyond isolated surrogate enzymes toward direct metabolite quantification and integrated pathway phenotyping.

Prospective studies should standardize collection time, anticoagulant, centrifugation, hemolysis assessment, and storage; use validated targeted mass-spectrometric or enzymatic methods; and report absolute NADPH and NADP concentrations together with their ratio and major related enzyme activities.
Longitudinal designs could then determine whether these measures track cognitive decline, established AD biomarkers, or treatment response.

Lessons from the implementation of blood-based amyloid and phosphorylated-tau biomarkers emphasize the importance of analytical validation, pre-analytical harmonization, and clinically defined use contexts [24] [25] [26].

text.text: This review explicitly separated direct NADP(H) measurements from pathway-related enzyme markers and stratified syntheses by disease stage, matrix, and analyte.
REML randomeffects models, modified Hartung-Knapp intervals, and sensitivity analyses were used to accommodate small and heterogeneous evidence sets.
Limitations include few poolable studies, nonuniform assays and units, graph-only outcomes, and an internally inconsistent report.

A formal risk-of-bias stratification was not performed; the results are therefore most appropriate for defining the direction of evidence and the principal research gap, rather than for establishing diagnostic thresholds.

text.text: Study characteristics and the direct-evidence gap 126 The 13 studies were published between 1996 and 2023.
Study groups included AD, MCI, 127 and, in some reports, vascular dementia as a differential-diagnosis comparator.
Specimens 128 included erythrocytes, whole blood, plasma, serum, lymphocytes, and other peripheral blood 129 cells.
GR was the most frequently measured enzyme, followed by G6PD/G6PDH and TRXR 130 (Table
Principal findings 176 This systematic review evaluated peripheral redox biology through the specific lens of NADP(H) metabolism.
Its clearest finding is that no eligible study directly measured peripheral NADPH, NADP , or the NADPH/NADP ratio.
The quantitative evidence instead concerns enzymes that generate or use NADPH.
Across these enzyme-based syntheses, pooled confidence intervals crossed the null and between-study heterogeneity was substantial.
The current literature therefore supports the presence of peripheral redox remodeling in AD and MCI, but not a reproducible unidirectional change in any single NADP(H)-related enzyme.
